articles.body: Volkswagen chief executive officer (CEO) Oliver Blume has called on European policymakers to establish the necessary regulatory framework to ensure the German automaker’s sweeping restructuring succeeds. According to a report by Reuters, addressing an event dubbed "For Europe" on the sidelines of the Paris motor show, Blume asked the European Union to make efforts to shield domestic industry from low-cost Chinese rivals.Volkswagen CEO's 'China warning' to European UnionBlume framed the turnaround as a collective duty, arguing that while corporations must sharpen their competitive edge and generate attractive business prospects, public officials are equally responsible for laying down viable operating conditions. "This is a shared responsibility: The business community must become more ⁠competitive and create attractive opportunities, while policymakers must establish the right framework conditions," he said.His views echo with that of Ford CEO Jim Farley who recently said that the US must carefully weigh how and whether Chinese automakers should enter ​the American market, and pointed to Europe as aThe remarks come at a time when Europe’s largest car manufacturer is undergoing the biggest-ever restructuring in its history. articles.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea
articles.summary: Latest missile launch appears to be a show of force since South Korea’s hypersonic missile test-fire, Seoul says.
articles.body:
North Korea has fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, South Korea’s military says.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said one of the missiles flew more than 900km (559 miles) from the Pyongyang area on Monday. The joint chiefs did not specify how many missiles were detected.

Japan’s coastguard said on Monday that North Korea had fired two unidentified projectiles, believed to be ballistic missiles, which appeared to have already fallen.

South Korea’s presidential office said that Pyongyang’s repeated missile launches violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, urging an immediate stop.

Monday’s missile launch adds to heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula, as both countries have been conducting weapons tests.

JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the latest missile launch appears to be a show of force since South Korea’s hypersonic missile test-fire.

On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.

Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.

On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.

Last week, Seoul demanded an apology after a landmine blast wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone between South and North Korea. A joint South Korean-UN investigation concluded that two landmines were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago. Pyongyang dismissed the claim and accused South Korea of provocation.

Prior to the border mine blast, Seoul said it was conducting “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between Pyongyang and Washington.

Lee pledged to reopen dialogue with North Korea in his first speech after taking office in 2025.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons programme, while rejecting US and South Korean offers to resume stalled diplomacy.

Talks between Kim and US President Donald Trump abruptly ended in 2019. Kim Jong Un’s government continues to demand that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearisation as a condition for talks.

articles.title: Buried bodies, cleared rubble, Israel’s yellow line: How war is hampering the search for Gaza’s missing
articles.summary: After three years of war, Palestinians are still searching for thousands of people reported missing in Gaza – many of whom are likely buried beneath the rubble.
articles.body: Dusk had fallen in the northern Gaza neighborhood of Jabalya when an Israeli quadcopter broke the evening lull on November 1, 2024. That evening, Mohammad Yousef Shalayel had settled into his in-laws’ home with his wife and children – after visiting 16 relatives displaced at his parents’ house nearby. He didn’t know that would be the last time they saw each other. An “enormous explosion” rocked the area, “completely collapsing” the Shalayel house. When Shalayel returned to the site of the attack the next morning, “all four floors had fallen on top of one another, on the people who were inside,” he said. Among them were his elderly mother, his two brothers and his sister, and their children and in-laws, too. “I will never forget… I found dismembered remains of children and women,” he told CNN in late September. “I broke down, but I tried to hold myself together so that I could gather the pieces of flesh that were scattered around.” Nearly two years later, Shalayel has been unable to return because the Israeli military has since occupied more than half of the shattered territory. He says almost all his family members remain unaccounted for. Amid the ruins of Gaza, Palestinians say they are trying to survive a conflict with no clear end in sight. Three years after Hamas and other militant groups killed around 1,200 people in Israel on October 7, 2023 – and a year after a US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the ensuing war in Gaza – Israeli strikes remain a near daily occurrence. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 74,000 people have been killed in the coastal enclave during the Israeli offensive. And the number may still rise significantly. Some 8,000 people are reported missing, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense, most of whom are likely buried beneath what the United Nations estimated last year to be 61 million tonnes of rubble. And with each day that passes, the chances of identifying the dead grow slimmer as “crucial evidence” is lost, said Pat Griffiths, a spokesman for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Jerusalem. Under international humanitarian law, the parties to an armed conflict “have an obligation to conduct search and recovery work” for the remains of those killed, missing or injured, and to collect, preserve and transfer that information to the other side, Griffiths told CNN. Access blocked Under the October 2025 ceasefire plan, Israeli forces were instructed to withdraw to the “yellow line,” which demarcated occupied areas. That shifting demarcation zone has blocked Palestinians from accessing swathes of land where their loved ones could be buried under the rubble, residents and aid workers say. Several people in Jabalya told CNN they witnessed the Israeli military demolishing mosques, homes and buildings or clearing rubble near the yellow line. “Where are the bones of our loved ones?” asked one resident, Yahya Odeh. “Where are their bodies? There are entire families beyond the yellow line who have been separated from their relatives.” In September, the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, warned against the clearance of rubble in areas under Israeli military control “by bulldozers with no respect for the dead,” after Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, a Geneva-based NGO, reported that such activity could erase evidence of war crimes. Türk said the recovery of “what appears to be entire families” from under the rubble in areas accessible to Palestinians highlights the need for evidence of possible war crimes to be preserved, and called for international investigators to be given access to all of Gaza. Meanwhile, Israel’s restrictions on heavy machinery entering Gaza have prolonged recovery efforts in parts of the enclave where Israeli troops are not currently present, Palestinian officials say. In August, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a 15-point plan laying out a pathway to long-term stability in Gaza, insisting Israel’s forces would not withdraw “until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.” The militant group in turn demanded that the Israeli military stop striking Gaza and pull back to the yellow line, as set out in the ceasefire plan. Last year, an independent UN inquiry found Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, a finding rejected by the Israeli government. Gaza City’s sole excavator In parts of Gaza accessible to Palestinians, Civil Defense members scour bombed-out homes for the remains of missing people. Since last October, field crews have recovered around 1,000 bodies from the rubble, according to Mahmoud Basal, the Civil Defense spokesperson. But only one excavator is available in Gaza City, with another in central Gaza, said Basal, adding that operations could be “completed” if Israeli authorities were to provide the 10 excavators, 10 bulldozers and 30 trucks requested by Palestinian officials. The Israeli aid agency tasked with facilitating the entry of aid into Gaza, COGAT, said Israel has allowed in “essential equipment” including engine oil, medical supplies and tents. However, COGAT insisted authorities would withhold heavy machinery and reconstruction materials until Hamas disarmed, according to Reuters. Recovery efforts are made more dangerous by the presence of unexploded ordnance, said Griffiths. Many rescue workers are “literally scraping away, a few centimeters at a time,” he added. When they do find buried Palestinians, some show signs of having been eaten by rodents or stray dogs, said Basal. Shalayel told CNN how he wrapped a blanket around his brother’s arm, which protruded from the rubble of their parents’ house, to try to protect it from an “enormous number” of roaming dogs. “It was a horrific sight,” he said. “In the end, the family tries to comfort itself by believing that all of its relatives have been recovered from beneath the rubble,” Basal said. “But we cannot state (that) with certainty.” Dr. Ahmad Dheir is one of only three remaining specialist forensic doctors in the enclave, he said. Even before the war, doctors had no access to DNA testing facilities, Dheir said, after a years-long blockade imposed by Israel and Egypt limited the entry of medical supplies. The slow eradication of Gaza’s medical infrastructure – following repeated Israeli strikes on health centers – has made medical workers even more reliant on elementary identification techniques, said Griffiths. When rescue teams deliver unidentified bodies to hospitals, the lack of freezer storage, fuel shortages and frequent power cuts hasten the deterioration of samples, said Dheir. With no DNA testing available, health workers have resorted to inconclusive blood typing and laboratory tests, condemning many relatives to a perpetual state of uncertainty, he said. ‘Deep human need for truth’ Suha al-Sharif’s son, Jihad, was supposed to care for his mother in old age. Instead, his absence is her only companion. “When Jihad left, I realized that he was the one carrying me. He was my strength,” the 55-year-old told CNN. Jihad, 33, was shot and killed on November 9, 2023 – when the family was displaced from Gaza City, Al-Sharif said. His body was taken to Al-Shifa Hospital, in the north, but Israel’s intensifying attacks meant health staffers could not bury people. Again, the family were forced to flee, journeying south. Nearly three years later, Al-Sharif has not been able to find him. “The hardest thing is that I couldn’t bury him; I don’t know where his body is,” she said. “At night, when I put my head on my pillow, memories come back,” she added. “There is nothing left to cry for. My life feels over.” Her sense of dispossession reflects that of many survivors in Gaza. Palestinians whose relatives are still missing have been presenting signs of “ambiguous loss” – a situational disorder where people feel lost, unable to concentrate, anxious, depressive or guilty, two aid workers told CNN. Some people pray, preserve photographs or loved ones’ belongings to “keep their memory alive,” according to Israa Alqahwaji, the mental health program coordinator in Gaza for the UK-based NGO Medical Aid for Palestinians. Wanting to find a person’s body “reflects a very deep human need for truth,” Alqahwaji said. “Continuing to live does not mean abandoning or forgetting the person they have lost,” she added. The cemetery of the missing In Deir al-Balah a cemetery of the missing, as locals call it, has become a totem for the unknown fate of hundreds of Palestinians. About 1,000 unidentified people have been buried there, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense. Authorities have been working with international aid agencies to build a digital information sharing system, ascribing serial numbers to unnamed graves so that if DNA testing becomes possible, loved ones may be able to identify their relatives in years to come. “We believe these people and their families have a right, as a matter of human dignity, to find their loved ones,” said Dheir. Shalayel hopes that one day he will find his family and lay them to rest with dignity. “For us, the people of Gaza, there is a well-known saying: Honoring the dead means burying them. Our religion, customs and traditions teach us that when someone dies, they should be buried, and their burial place should be known.”

articles.title: Pope Leo denounces death penalty as 'inadmissible' ahead of Pentagon's planned livestreamed execution
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV called the death penalty "inadmissible" on World Day Against the Death Penalty after the Pentagon announced plans to livestream an execution.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV condemned the death penalty as "inadmissible" as the Pentagon faces criticism over plans to livestream an execution later this year. Leo, the first American pope, shared his opposition to capital punishment Saturday in a social media post marking World Day Against the Death Penalty. Citing Catholic doctrine revised under his predecessor, Pope Francis, Leo emphasized that the death penalty violates human dignity. "The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo wrote on X. "#NoDeathPenalty," he added in the post. VETERAN SHOT 7 TIMES IN FORT HOOD MASSACRE HAS A WARNING FOR AMERICANS PLANNING TO WATCH EXECUTION In 2018, Francis revised the Catholic Church's official position on capital punishment, declaring the death penalty "inadmissible" in all circumstances. "Consequently the church teaches, in the light of the Gospel, that the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person," the revised Catechism states. Before the change, Catholic teaching permitted the death penalty in cases where it was deemed the only effective means of protecting human life from a dangerous offender. Earlier popes had maintained that exception, though Pope John Paul II increasingly advocated ending capital punishment, stressing that those convicted of crimes retain their human dignity. Although Leo did not specifically mention the U.S. government's plans in his statement, his post comes after the Pentagon announced on Thursday that it had scheduled a firing squad execution for a man convicted of a mass shooting at a military base. Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base. He is set to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, which would make him the first person to be executed by firing squad by the U.S. military since 1945. President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had not yet decided whether to allow the livestream plan, pushed by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, to move forward. Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic, expressed skepticism about whether the Pentagon would proceed with a public execution. He said he would not watch the livestream if it were carried out. Several lawmakers, including Republicans, have spoken out against plans to broadcast the execution. CHRISTA PIKE DISCHARGED FROM HOSPITAL, RETURNED TO PRISON AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION, ATTORNEYS SAY "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said on Thursday. "It should not be happening in America." Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, criticized the proposed broadcast, calling it "truly incomprehensible" and warning that it was "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle." "The Church’s position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent," Parolin told reporters on Friday. "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don’t know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods." He added that the death penalty "is incompatible with human dignity and does not serve as a deterrent." The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" about the public execution plan and urged the U.S. to reconsider. "In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement on Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people." Pike survived the attempted execution despite two doses of pentobarbital being administered late last month. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: China sanctions Paraguay, Belize ministers over Taiwan ties
articles.summary: Chinese Foreign Ministry cites national sovereignty and Taiwan separatist activities as reasons behind the measures.
articles.body:
China has sanctioned Paraguay’s communications minister and Belize’s foreign minister over ties to Taiwan.

The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs made the announcement on Monday, citing the safeguarding of China’s national sovereignty and opposition to Taiwan separatist activities as the reasons behind the measures, which went into effect the same day.

The measures against Paraguay’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate and Belize’s Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca include the freezing of their assets in China and the denial of entry visas to Hong Kong and Macau.

The sanctions also prohibit Chinese organisations and individuals from engaging in transactions, cooperation or other activities with the ministers.

The Foreign Ministry said that “certain anti-China politicians” who are “driven by self-interest” have pushed their nations to maintain diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

Beijing said the ministers had “taken a series of egregious actions and statements”, which are “damaging China’s core interests”.

Paraguay and Belize are two of 12 countries that maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

China views Taiwan as its territory, a view the island’s government strongly rejects.

The measures come two days after Taiwan’s National Day celebration.

In a National Day speech outside the Presidential Office on Saturday, Taiwan President William Lai Ching-te said the island “cherishes peace” and will “not give up our freedom”.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office condemned Lai’s speech, saying it “disregards facts, ⁠distorts the truth, misleads the public, and reveals ulterior motives”.

In January, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to achieve the “reunification” of China and Taiwan, calling the goal “unstoppable”.

Paraguay’s Communications Minister Villate marked Taiwan’s National Day with a social media post, saying: “Paraguay reaffirms its relationship of friendship and cooperation, based on shared values and principles: the self-determination of peoples, human rights and democracy.”

The Belize embassy in Taiwan also posted a message on its Facebook celebrating the 37th anniversary of their diplomatic relations.

“Together, we look forward to a future of growth, opportunity, and lasting friendship,” the embassy wrote.

Last month, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize. His ministry said the two sides had agreed to deepen ties.

Taiwan’s other allies in the Americas include Guatemala and Haiti. It also has formal diplomatic ties with three Caribbean islands.

The United States does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but Washington is bound by law to provide the island with the means to ‌defend itself.

Earlier this month, the US delivered two fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack from China .

articles.title: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth
articles.summary: Backdated paperwork also made the Russian oligarch’s yachts and mansions disappear from accounts, BBC finds.
articles.body:
The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.

Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.

Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.

Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.

Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".

The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.

The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".

Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.

The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022.

The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation.

In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false.

The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city.

Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune.

The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices.

Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth.

Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property.

A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus.

To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003.

Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts.

When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained.

Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading.

Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.

Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.

This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.

It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.

But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.

An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.

MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.

A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".

MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.

This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.

Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.

So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.

Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.

Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."

In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.

MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.

It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.

Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.

MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.

Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents."

Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal."

Denying any wrongdoing by the oligarch, Roman Abramovich's lawyers said that he was "not involved in the day-to-day operation of those companies" and that where arrangements were proposed by professional advisers, "reliance on that advice was entirely proper and legitimate".

Deloitte Cyprus said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.

MeritServus closed following the Cyprus Confidential leak.

articles.title: Rejecting closer EU ties would be dereliction of duty, PM to say
articles.summary: Addressing the Commons, Burnham is expected to say that a new deal with the EU could help tackle illegal immigration and boost economic growth.
articles.body:
The prime minister is expected to tell the Commons later it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn down a closer relationship with the European Union - if one can be negotiated with Brussels.

In a statement to MPs on Monday, Andy Burnham will argue it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain."

He first pledged to explore closer ties with the bloc at a UK-EU summit later this year at the Labour Party conference last month.

Addressing the Commons, Burnham is expected to say that a new deal with the EU could help tackle illegal immigration and boost economic growth.

He will claim that if he could secure that then "the vast majority of the public would expect us to take it".

Last month, Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" a future Labour election manifesto could promise a new in-out referendum on the EU.

A summit between the UK and the EU was due to take place in the summer but was postponed after Sir Keir Starmer announced his resignation. It has been rescheduled for next month.

The prime minister hopes to secure tweaks to the current arrangements between London and Brussels and also begin a wider conversation about the long term relationship between the UK and its nearest neighbours.

A No 10 source said: "Andy understands why some politicians don't want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised.

"But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be. Sticking with the status quo and not working relentlessly to secure a good deal that boosts growth would be a major dereliction of duty."

In his speech at Labour's conference, he said "immigration control" had been "weakened by Brexit" because the UK "lost collaboration with our European partners. And we are still having to work hard to bring it back".

Speaking at her party conference last week, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said it was "a terrible idea" to "reopen the Brexit debate."

"Can you imagine having to go through that again? So much time lost, arguing with ourselves with the EU. Going round in circles, businesses not knowing whether they should invest. He wants to do it all again."

The Commons sits on Monday for the first time since 15 September, having been in recess during some of the party conferences.

articles.title: Macbeth to be staged at Oldham's last nightclub Liquid and Envy
articles.summary: Shakespeare's famous play will be performed at the nightclub in an effort to engage "new audiences".
articles.body:
While the Oldham Coliseum Theatre's doors remain closed during its major revamp, the creative team has needed to think outside the box when deciding where to temporarily decamp.

They have chosen the last remaining nightclub in the Greater Manchester town to stage William Shakespeare's Macbeth.

"I want to blow the dust off Shakespeare," said the Coliseum's new creative director Nick Bagnall.

"This isn't about putting the play on a pedestal, it's about creating an experience that grabs people by the throat, whether they have seen Macbeth 10 times or never encountered it before.

"We want people who have never set foot in a theatre to walk into Liquid and Envy and feel this story belongs to them.

"Staging Macbeth inside a working Oldham nightclub creates its own intrigue."

This will be a different experience for the actors too, moving from the stage to the to a once sticky dancefloor covered in spilled drinks.

Andy Sheridan, who plays Macbeth, has previously appeared in HBO's Industry as well as Channel 4's The Couple Next Door.

He said: "I think it's really important for Oldham to set such an important play that is so famous in an iconic venue in this town.

The audience will be seated in the booths and stools to watch the show, which has shifted the action to the 1970s world of gangsters, casinos and shifting social codes.

The aim was to create a performance of Macbeth that feels closer to a night out than a night at the theatre, without losing the force of Shakespeare's language.

Martina Murphy, the Coliseum's chief executive, said: "This is a huge moment for the Coliseum.

"Nick's Macbeth is uncompromising, thrilling and unmistakably of this place, and it announces exactly the kind of theatre we intend to make.

"As we continue our journey back to Fairbottom Street, we are determined to keep creating ambitious work that surprises audiences and reaches people wherever they are."

Oldham's Coliseum Theatre is being refurbished after a long campaign to save the venue, backed by former Coronation Street actor Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The theatre is now expected to reopen in 2027 after securing an extra £7m grant to clear the asbestos and fix structural defects beneath a staircase.

Macbeth runs at Liquid and Envy in Oldham from 23 October to 7 November.

articles.title: Why did Pakistan declare Emergency in Imran Khan's bastion Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
articles.summary: Pakistan's political battle with jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has taken a sharp turn, with the Shehbaz Sharif government suspending his
articles.body: Pakistan's political battle with jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has taken a sharp turn, with the Shehbaz Sharif government suspending his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led administration in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and imposing governor's rule in the province.The move brings one of Imran Khan's strongest political strongholds under direct control of the Shehbaz Sharif-led government, further deepening the confrontation between the military-backed government and PTI.Amid growing insecurities within the Shehbaz Sharif-Asim Munir duo, Imran Khan’s party has lost control of a province with around 40 million people, turning the region into the latest flashpoint in Pakistan’s political unrest.Thousands of people have taken to the streets in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since early October, demanding Imran Khan’s release and protesting the military’s counter-insurgency operations along the border with Afghanistan.The Pakistan government has defended the move, citing the worsening law and order situation and accusing the provincial administration of failing to act against terrorism. Militants linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), an ideological ally of the Afghan Taliban, have killed thousands of security personnel and civilians in recent years.“The Cabinet took a detailed review of the deteriorating law and order situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the circumstances arising from the provincial government’s deliberate indifference in the war against terrorism,” the office of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said in a statement.However, figures compiled by the Islamabad-based Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS) paint a different picture of the security situation in the province, as Financial Times reported.Civilian and security personnel deaths in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa stood at 485 in the first nine months of 2026, down 16% from the same period in 2025. Across Pakistan, such deaths rose by 9%, according to the think-tank.Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari approved the emergency on the prime minister’s advice. His office cited a “failure of negotiations” between the Pakistan government and PTI leaders in the province.Under governor’s rule, the governor, who is appointed by the Pakistan government, takes over the province’s administration. Pakistan’s interior ministry said the army would deploy personnel to help run the province and protect public property and government installations.Talal Chaudhry, junior interior minister, told the Financial Times that the move was a “routine measure” intended to help provincial authorities carry out their responsibilities, particularly in the fight against terrorism.PTI leaders arrested after emergency announcementThe political confrontation intensified soon after the announcement, with reports emerging that senior PTI leaders had been arrested.An account on X associated with Junaid Akbar, a member of parliament and president of PTI’s provincial chapter, said he and provincial chief minister Sohail Afridi had been taken into custody.Afridi, 37, had been leading a long march across the province in support of Khan and against military operations that PTI claims have caused civilian deaths and damage. He is the youngest-ever chief minister of Pakistan and comes from the tribal belt bordering Afghanistan.Just hours before his government was suspended, Afridi had vowed to continue the march until the protesters’ demands were met.“There is no option other than accepting our demands,” Afridi said in a post on X.“We will not back down,” he said. “Our long march will continue until the demands are met, in accordance with the law. Here, only Imran Khan’s policy will prevail.”Pakistan’s interior ministry and armed forces did not respond to requests for comment, the Financial Times reported.Imran Khan’s stronghold at the centre of political battleKhyber Pakhtunkhwa has been a key political base for Imran Khan's PTI, which has governed the province since 2013. The party won more than 60% of the seats in the provincial assembly in the 2024 elections, two years after Khan was removed as prime minister through a parliamentary no-confidence vote.The former World Cup-winning cricket captain continues to be widely regarded as Pakistan’s most popular politician. Candidates backed by him won the largest number of seats in the national assembly in 2024.However, they were kept out of power as the military and the country’s two dominant dynastic political parties shaped the post-election arrangement, according to the Financial Times.The FT also cited analysts as saying PTI would comfortably win a competitive general election.PTI has accused the Shehbaz Sharif government of using security concerns as a pretext to remove its elected administration in the province.“The arrest of chief minister Sohail Afridi and Junaid Akbar has exposed the political nature of the government’s actions,” PTI spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram said in a statement.“These measures are not directed at addressing security challenges; they are intended to weaken PTI, undermine the elected government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and disregard the democratic will of its people.”You use AI every day. articles.title: New Forest tourist tax: How would a visitor levy work?
articles.summary: Businesses fear it would deter families, while conservationists want the money spent locally.
articles.body:
Holidaymakers in the New Forest could one day be paying a tourist tax on their accommodation under new government plans.

The levy would be optional, with areas able to choose whether to have one, how much to charge and how the money is spent.

One of the area's biggest holiday park operators has said it is "strongly opposed" to the tax, warning that it could deter tourists from visiting the area.

But conservation groups say a levy could help protect the national park if the money is spent in the right way.

The government confirmed its plans in September, following a public consultation, and intends to bring in the legislation during this Parliament.

The levy would be charged as a percentage of the cost of an overnight stay, excluding meals and other extras.

It would apply to hotels, B&Bs, holiday parks, holiday lets and short-term lets such as Airbnb. Day visitors would not pay.

Accommodation businesses would be responsible for paying it, but could pass some or all of the cost on to guests.

The decision would rest with the new Hampshire and the Solent authority, which does not yet have a mayor.

Its first mayoral election is due in 2028, although the authority has asked for it to be brought forward to 2027.

Under the government's rules, any levy would have to apply at a single rate across the whole authority area, meaning the New Forest could not be charged differently from Southampton or Portsmouth.

Authorities would not be allowed to vary the rate by season, and there would be no discount for local residents.

The money raised would not have to be spent on tourism, or in the area where it was raised.

Shorefield Holidays, which runs holiday parks in Hampshire and Dorset, said a levy would "add another cost to family holidays at a time when people are already facing significant increases in the cost of living".

"An additional charge could make some people think twice about visiting the New Forest or choose a different destination altogether," it said.

The company said that while the levy would be collected by businesses, the cost would ultimately have to be passed on to guests or absorbed, at a time when its own costs were rising.

New Forest West MP Sir Desmond Swayne has also opposed the plans, telling the Commons that if hoteliers in Bournemouth were "gagging to pay this tax" , those in the New Forest were not.

More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

Sarah Nield, chair of the New Forest Association, said the group did not have a position on whether there should be a levy, but if one was introduced, some of the money should be "ploughed back" into the national park.

"Tourists come to this area because of the qualities of the national park," she said. "National park finances are not particularly healthy."

She said the Forest faced recreational pressure from millions of visitors a year, adding: "The place isn't free... it does require management, it does require rangers."

"If that money could go back to supporting the national park, I think that could in a way benefit everybody," she said.

Is there already a visitor contribution?

The New Forest Trust already runs a voluntary Visitor Gift Scheme, which Nield described as "an embryonic type of tourist tax".

About 45 local businesses invite guests to add a donation to their stay, which goes towards conservation projects in the Forest.

The government said the levy would allow areas to invest in attractions and the visitor experience, bringing more overnight stays and benefiting the businesses that pay it.

articles.title: Regional policing unit drops controversial Palantir AI technology
articles.summary: Five police forces decide not to continue using software from a US tech firm after a two-year trial
articles.body:
A regional policing unit dedicated to tackling serious and organised crime has decided not to continue using software from the controversial US tech giant Palantir after a two-year trial.

The US firm's technology, which allows large data sets to be analysed and searched easily, including through the use of AI, is being used by militaries and public services across the world.

East Midlands Special Operations Unit (Emsou) said it started a trial in October 2024 to see how well Palantir's software could help it investigate crime without compromising ethics or accountability.

But it has decided not to fund a new contract and told the BBC Palantir will now have to demonstrate it has cut all links with the force's systems and has deleted all of its data.

Protestors regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and opposition to its use in US immigration enforcement.

Privacy experts have also raised concerns that its tools enable surveillance and analysis of everything from social media posts to driving licences and DNA swabs.

But the company says its software has delivered better public services across UK organisations which include the NHS, the ministry of defence and 11 police forces.

Emsou, which investigates crimes including murder, terrorism offences and drug trafficking in Derbyshire, Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire and Northamptonshire, declined to disclose how exactly it used Palantir's technology during the pilot.

But it has confirmed the trial fed data from Leicestershire Police into an operating system called Foundry that uses artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Palantir provided the BBC with a number of examples of how other forces had used its software to fight crime.

"This includes helping to improve the enforcement of Clare's Law by identifying 1,000 women in Bedfordshire whose partners have a history of domestic violence in a single year," a spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added it had also helped to convict a criminal gang that stole £700,000 from cash machines and helped the Metropolitan Police root out serious corruption and identify significant time savings.

Regional Assistant Chief Constable Ian Green said the East Midlands trial aimed to test how well the software could serve the public interest "while upholding the highest standards of accountability and ethics".

He added the trial was conducted with strict "checks, balances and independent review" but Emsou decided not to renew the contract after its Home Office funding ended.

"Following the scoping work and assessment of what it would deliver, including our future funding streams, we have taken the decision not to take the project further," he said.

"We continue to embrace innovation and look at how new technology can support us in policing, and we will continue to explore new ways of targeting serious organised crime in our region and beyond."

Emsou said it could not disclose which datasets and sources were used during the trial for "operational security" and would not reveal the cost due to commercial confidentiality.

The Home Office did not want to add to Emsou's statement.

Palantir's critics have also raised concerns about its AI-enabled "war-fighting" technology.

The US has reportedly used Palantir's defence platform, Maven Smart System , to plan strikes across Iran in the last few months.

The firm faced questions over whether Maven might recommend incorrect targets - which could include civilians - and whether time-pressured commanders may not question those suggestions sufficiently.

Palantir said the company's role is only to provide software.

"How that software is used is entirely under the control of the customer with data only able to be processed in accordance with their strict instructions," a spokesperson said.

Palantir said NHS Trusts using its software had performed thousands of additional operations, reduced discharge times and improved the speed of diagnosis.

It said they include the University Hospitals of Leicester and Sherwood Forest Hospitals Trusts.

But Amnesty International UK is campaigning against a large NHS England contract with Palantir over its concerns about the firm’s impact on human rights.

In a statement, the charity's military, security and policy director, Oliver Feeley-Sprague, welcomed Emsou's decision to stop using Palantir Foundry.

"People want policing that serves communities, not controversial contractors," he said.

"Palantir has become a growing liability for any public body that values human rights and public confidence."

articles.title: Locals 'shocked, angry and scared' by Oxfordshire solar plan
articles.summary: Developer Low Carbon says the 2,400 acre West Oxfordshire Energy Plant would produce 500MW.
articles.body:
People living near the proposed site of a huge new solar farm have told the BBC they are "shocked, angry and very scared" by the plans.

Developer Low Carbon said the 2,400 acre West Oxfordshire Energy Plant (WOEP) would produce 500MW - enough electricity to power 145,000 homes.

Three of the UK's biggest solar farms are now being planned for Oxfordshire, with the government considering the proposal for the 840MW Botley West project, and another 500MW solar farm proposed for Wantage area .

Low Carbon said it was "here to listen" to local concerns, and that there would be a public consultation in the new year.

But Michael Ergatoudis, whose home in Grafton backs onto the proposed site, said residents were "very shocked" to "suddenly find that we'll be living in an ocean of solar panels".

Meanwhile, Kate Eavis said she was feeling "pretty anxious" that the scheme would be built next to her home in Little Faringdon.

"The countryside around here is very much a part of my daily life and I feel that that is going to be taken away and replaced by effectively a sort of industrial landscape," she said.

Last year, solar energy provided more than 6% of Britain's electricity – rising to more than 40% for a small number of half-hour periods in July.

Because the development would generate more than 100MW of power, it will bypass the usual planning route - with a decision instead resting with the energy secretary and Planning Inspectorate.

Jim Johnston, from Langford, said he was not "anti-solar" but was concerned by the scale of the plans.

"What's proposed will completely transform an agricultural and rural environment to an industrial one," he said.

Fellow Langford resident Tom Marshall agreed that he had "no objection to a small solar farm or a field with solar panels in it".

"But when it completely surrounds your village and other villages in the area, then that's a different thing altogether."

The number of landowners contributing to WOEP is currently unknown, but some UK farmers see solar as a profitable alternative to agriculture or raising livestock.

Ed Perrin, Low Carbon's development director, said the firm had "already undertaken a number of surveys" over the past year and was "already getting a good understanding of the nature that exists within the site at present".

"Our design process is about ensuring that nature and landscape impacts are considered right from the outset, it's very much a nature and landscape-led design," he said.

"Our objective at Low Carbon is to make sure that our projects have a better environment than we started with."

Low Carbon said it was looking to submit a planning application for the site by the end of 2027, and hoped to start construction "in the early part of the next decade".

But Langford resident George Leavey said the firm would encounter "a lot of determined people here who are going to really work together as a community and really fight this thing".

He added: "I think everyone here is up for the fight."

articles.title: Rural West communities struggle as price of heating oil rises
articles.summary: The rural communities vulnerable to heating oil prices rises as the weather gets colder.
articles.body:
As the temperature drops, some of us will start putting the heating on but for the one-and-a-half million people across the UK that are not on the mains gas network - and who are relying instead on heating oil - that decision may give them pause.

The vast majority of those people live in rural locations.

The heating oil market is unregulated, unlike gas and electricity, so any changes in the global price quickly gets passed on to customers .

Tensions in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine are two issues currently both affecting supply which is causing prices to rise.

Until March this year, the price was quite stable at about 60p per litre (ppl) but when the war in Iran started in March, it jumped to a high of 134ppl .

After a dip in the past few months, it is rising once again and it currently stands at 111ppl, according to price comparison site Boiler Juice.

The BBC has spoken to a number of business and homeowners across the West about how that rise is affecting them.

Peter Mason lives in Minety, in north Wiltshire, where most homes rely on heating oil.

"I'm getting toward the end of the tank and need to top up for winter... it will be over £550," he said.

Mason said that last year "it was about £300 to fill up - it is horrendous".

He said: "The price goes up and down. It can vary plus or minus £50 but it has never been as high as it is today.

"It means I'll have to eek out what I spent my money on. I'm retired, its not like I can change jobs.

"I have to be really careful and pull money out of savings."

Dylan Williams owns van-driving business Van & I of Monmouth, Wales and regularly operates in the Forest of Dean, Stroud and South Gloucestershire.

The 51-year-old said he was currently paying more for fuel than he ever had in the three years of running his business.

He said he had had to put the prices of his services up to offset the rise.

At the start of the year he would pay between £120 and £130 for a full tank, he said, but that had now gone up to £160.

"It's ever increasing, ever worrying - keeping an eye on the news, keeping an eye on the diesel prices," he said.

"I mean I've got fuel cards... you don't pay the pump prices, you pay the fuel card prices but it doesn't make much a difference these days.

Yvette Farrell, volunteer director for Dean Forest Kitchen, which cook fresh meals every day and delivers them to clients within the Forest of Dean, said they might have to increase prices as there's "not going to be much choice in the future".

She said: "It's impacted us a lot because we work on a not-for-profit scenario so there is not a lot of wiggle room when it comes to increase in any expenses.

"So the cost of fuel is really, really hitting the business hard and we're having to do our best to still keep going to our clients who are spread across a very rural area with no public transport.

"But we have to take these meals to them because... they will not have somebody coming to see them during the day because they're so isolated."

Tristan Holland, company director at TLC Support Service, manages a small team of community care workers who travel around Wotton-under-Edge and Dursley.

Staff use their own vehicles and the company pays mileage at 55p per business mile.

He said: "We had an increase in our fees back at the start of the year, just kind of taking into account all the extras that were coming in this year but even that does make it tight.

"Everything has risen - the cost of the fuel, the training, even the uniforms that we purchased.

"Everything has gone up and so we try to keep our services as affordable as we possibly can but there has to be a profit or else we just can't carry on going."

The Iran war has disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and prices can rise or fall based on the words and actions of key political figures.

It is thought prices could come down if there is a peace deal between the US and Iran.

For people who rely on heating oil, it means feeling helpless.

Richard Willan, who runs the Nadder Oil Buying Club in Wiltshire where more than 1,000 residents buy in bulk together to get a better price, said rural residents were increasingly vulnerable as the colder months set in.

"We are watching to see what happens with (Donald) Trump in the mid-term elections in America, that might change things again," he said.

The Competitions and Markets Authority (CMA) said heating oil customers in remote areas were too vulnerable to price shocks.

CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell said: "Stronger safeguards are needed - including regulatory oversight and better support for vulnerable consumers as well as communities living in areas of the UK that are particularly exposed to higher and more volatile prices."

As prices sit above 100ppl with the temperature falling, there are calls for more support for rural communities.

Chief Executive of Action in Rural Communities England Corinne Pluchino said: "Without specific targeted support for heating oil and LPG users, thousands of rural people risk becoming the forgotten victims of the energy crisis."

The organisation is asking the government to remove VAT on heating oil and LPG for six months in this month's budget.

There are also locally-run support schemes like the Surviving Winter campaign run by a group of charities in Wiltshire which supported more than 3,000 people last year with the cost of heating.

A spokesperson for the Department for the Environment and Net Zero said: "We are helping thousands of households on heating oil switch to clean heat with grants worth £9,000, alongside a dedicated resilience fund for areas with higher rates of oil heating.

articles.title: INDIA bloc fumes as CJI declines meeting request; Raut says ‘people will remember this’
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Several opposition leaders from the INDIA bloc criticised Chief Justice of India (CJI) Justice Surya Kant after he declined Lok Sabha LoP Rahul
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Several opposition leaders from the INDIA bloc criticised Chief Justice of India (CJI) Justice Surya Kant after he declined Lok Sabha LoP Rahul Gandhi’s request for a meeting to discuss alleged electoral fraud and the deletion of voters’ names from electoral rolls.Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut questioned the decision, saying the bloc wanted to raise concerns about “theft of votes” and the impact of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition’s reaction came as the INDIA bloc has planned a protest march towards the Supreme Court on Monday.Raut said the Chief Justice’s refusal to meet the leaders would be remembered by the people, while Congress MP Imran Masood described the planned protest as a spontaneous movement.“We have come today as the INDIA bloc is organising a major march towards the Supreme Court to meet the Chief Justice. We had requested an appointment... The Chief Justice, whose role is to safeguard the Constitution, is unwilling to meet us... When we are seeking to save democracy amidst the theft of votes and electoral fraud, and the deletion of millions of names from the rolls and wish to meet you to voice our grievance, you say you will not meet politicians. The people will remember this,” Raut said.Congress MP Imran Masood also said the party had scheduled a protest and that members would follow the leadership’s directions.“We have scheduled a protest. Everyone will abide by whatever directive the party issues. People are coming out on their own; everywhere it is a spontaneous movement,” Masood said.Meanwhile, DMK spokesperson T K S Elangovan questioned the circumstances behind the CJI’s decision to decline the meeting request and alleged that the Election Commission was not acting neutrally.“I do not know what pressure they are under... It is a petition in favour of democracy. We complain that Gyanesh Kumar is pro-BJP and he does not act neutrally... They should act neutrally, only then democracy will survive. If they are supporting Gyanesh Kumar, that means they are also against democracy...” Elangovan said.CJI denies meeting requestResponding to the meeting request, Justice Surya Kant said he had received a letter seeking an appointment on Sunday and had replied the same night, explaining why he would be unable to meet the leaders.“I received a letter yesterday regarding a meeting request, and I responded to it last night, outlining the reasons why I will be unable to meet...” the CJI said.He also stressed that citizens and elected representatives could approach the court through legal channels.“The Supreme Court's doors are open to everyone. Any petition from any common citizen or member of an elected body is welcome. Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
